title: BikeWatch: Boston Bike Traffic Explorer
description: An interactive map visualizing Bluebikes traffic patterns across Boston and Cambridge, including time-of-day filtering, station flow direction, and isochrone accessibility analysis.
story: I was interested in how movement through a city changes over the course of a day, not just in volume but in direction and accessibility. This project became a way to layer those dynamics together—using time filtering, directional flow, and isochrones to make patterns in commuting and urban access more legible. It reinforced my interest in using interactive visualization not just to display data, but to surface relationships that are otherwise hard to see.

title: Charging Ahead: V2G School Bus Thesis
description: Master’s thesis modeling the feasibility and grid value of vehicle-to-grid electric school buses in California.
story: I wanted to study a climate solution that was both technically interesting and grounded in public benefit. Electric school buses stood out because they are batteries on wheels, but also because they sit idle for long stretches and serve communities directly. This project pushed me to connect power system modeling, transportation behavior, and policy design into one story about what a more participatory energy transition could look like.

title: CAISO Dispatch and Emissions Analysis
description: Analysis of dispatch, ramping, and fossil generator emissions using GenX outputs and EPA CEMS data.
story: I kept returning to the question of what grid flexibility actually displaces in practice. It is easy to say storage reduces emissions, but much harder to trace that claim through hourly operations and fossil plant behavior. This project became a way to connect model outputs to real generator-level emissions patterns and ask whether reducing ramping stress could produce measurable environmental gains.

title: Advancing Massachusetts Power Grant Research
description: Policy research and stakeholder analysis for a Massachusetts storage and resilience grant program.
story: What interested me most was not just where money should go, but how programs decide what counts as value in the first place. Through this work, I thought deeply about community benefits, permitting barriers, and which organizations are empowered to shape project design. The project reinforced my belief that implementation details are never neutral; they determine who a clean energy transition is really for.

title: Housing Justice in Greater Boston
description: Research project examining investor ownership, vacancies, and housing justice across Boston-area submarkets.
story: This project started from a frustration with how abstract housing conversations can become. I wanted to map ownership patterns in a way that made displacement pressures and neighborhood inequality more visible. Working through the data made clear that categories like vacancy, ownership, and investment are not just technical variables; they are part of a larger story about power, extraction, and who gets to stay in the city.

title: COVID-19 Visualization Redesign
description: Data visualization assignment redesigning COVID-19 case graphics to better communicate seasonality and scale.
story: I was drawn to the challenge of how visual design shapes emotional interpretation. Rather than treating charts as neutral containers for numbers, I wanted to think about pacing, annotation, and visual emphasis as rhetorical choices. This project helped me articulate a broader principle I keep returning to: the form of a visualization is part of the argument it makes.

title: Interactive Portfolio Website
description: Personal website built with Svelte to showcase projects, writing, and technical work.
story: I wanted a space that felt more alive than a static resume. Building the site became a small design exercise in how to present technical work without stripping away the values and motivations behind it. Every layout choice made me ask the same question: what do I want people to understand about the kind of researcher and builder I am?

title: School Bus Fleet Electrification Explorer
description: Exploratory analysis of school bus fleet data, vehicle replacement timing, and electrification opportunities.
story: Before I had a full thesis framing, I was trying to understand the basic landscape: where the buses were, how old they were, and what an electrification opportunity might even mean in practice. This project was less polished than later work, but it was where the bigger research story began. It taught me that good modeling questions often start with descriptive curiosity.

title: Energy Systems Modeling with PyPSA-USA
description: Scenario analysis using PyPSA-USA to study grid operations, prices, and decarbonization pathways.
story: I was fascinated by how large, complex systems can be represented through carefully structured data and constraints. Working with PyPSA-USA gave me a way to see how assumptions around fuels, transmission, and technology costs ripple through an entire modeled grid. It also made me more attentive to the politics hidden inside modeling defaults and data pipelines.

title: Community Energy Resilience StoryMap
description: A narrative mapping project on local energy resilience, public infrastructure, and climate vulnerability.
story: I wanted to experiment with a format that felt more accessible than a report and more grounded than a dashboard. The result was a narrative map that connected place-based vulnerability with questions of energy resilience and public investment. It reminded me that storytelling is not a layer added after analysis; it is one of the ways analysis becomes meaningful to other people.
